The Jefferson Administration. In principle, the Framers were 
antagonistic to the spirit of party or faction, and it is Andrew Jackson in 
the 1820s who is usually credited with creating a federal spoils system in 
which appointed offices could legitimately be filled based on partisan 
allegiance. The transition from the Federalist John Adams to Democratic- 
Repubhcan Thomas Jefferson, however, marked the first party turnover in 
the presidency. Despite Jefferson’s reputation for pohtical moderation, a 
thorough study of his personnel practices reveals that “[r]emovals in one 
form or another for purely political reasons constituted the backbone of 
[Jefferson’s] effort to break the Federafists’ power.” Carl E. Prince, The 
Passing of the Aristocracy: Jefferson’s Removal of the Federalists, 1801— 
1805, 57 J. Am. His t . 563 (1970). Jefferson also took advantage of 
appointment process technicalities to prevent some Federalists from taking 
office—^most famously, William Marbury, whose undelivered commission 
Jefferson withheld. In Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. 137, 162 (1803), Chief 
Justice John Marshall wrote that because “the law creating the office [of 
justice of the peace], gave the officer a right to hold for five years, 
independent of the executive, the appointment was not revocable,” 
meaning that Jefferson would have been without power formally to remove 
Marbury. (Although accurate in its time, Jane Manners & Lev Menand, 
The Three Permissions: Presidential Removal and the Statutory Limits of 
Agency Independence, 121 COLUM. L. Re v . 1, 25 (2021), the statutory 
specification of a term of years without more may now be interpreted as 
consistent with at-will removability during the specified term.)
Jackson and the National Bank. Andrew Jackson’s cArnpaign against 
the Second National Bank of the United States famously included his veto 
of the 1832 Act that would have granted an early renewal of that Rank’s 
charter. Jackson’s statement asserted that, as President, he was entitled 
to judge the constitutionality of the bank independently of Congress and 
the Supreme Court. (The Court had held the bank charter constitutional in 
McCulloch V. Maryland, VI U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316 (1819)). After winning the 
1832 election, Jackson determined to weaken the bank even before the 
expiration of its charter by removing federal deposits and transferring 
federal funds to state banks. Because Louis M^cLane, his treasury 
secretary, was a defender of the bank, Jackson’s first step in laying the 
groundwork for his plan was to nominate McLane to become Secretary of 
State, thus getting him out of the way politically. Jackson appointed as 
McLane’s replacement a bank opponent, William Duane, who, as it turned 
out, was nonetheless opposed to the funds transfer.
